Book of Sports
bŏk əv sports
n. (the royal Declaration of Sports of James I, 1618, reissued by Charles I in 1633, permitting recreations on the Lord's Day)
Old English boc, book; Middle English disport, recreation, from Old French desporter, to divert.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Book of Sports was a royal declaration first issued by James I for Lancashire in 1617, after a quarrel between Puritan magistrates and Catholic gentry over Sunday games, and extended to the whole kingdom in 1618. It declared that after divine service on the Lord's Day the people should not be hindered from lawful recreations such as dancing, archery, leaping, vaulting, May games, Whitsun ales, morris dances, and the setting up of maypoles, though bear-baiting, bull-baiting, interludes, and bowling remained forbidden. James had meant to have it read in every church but withdrew the order. In 1633 Charles I, at the urging of William Laud, reissued the declaration and required the clergy to read it from their pulpits. Many Puritan ministers refused; some read it and then read the fourth commandment after it; a number were suspended or deprived, and the controversy did much to drive godly men toward emigration and toward Parliament. In 1643 Parliament ordered the book publicly burned by the hangman. The ministers who would not read it stood on the commandment, “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8), and on Isaiah's description of the day kept “not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure” (Isa 58:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sport as play, diversion, or that which diverts and makes mirth, and the sabbath as the day of rest.

expand to see more

SPORT, n. That which diverts and makes mirth; pastime; diversion; play.

SAB'BATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest; among christians, the first day of the week, in commemoration of the resurrection of Christ.

DECLARA'TION, n. A proclamation or affirmation; publication.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:8 — "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy."

Isa 58:13 — "If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the LORD, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:"

Rev 1:10 — "I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day, and heard behind me a great voice, as of a trumpet,"

Act 5:29 — "Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men."

Modern Corruption

A royal order to the clergy to proclaim Sunday sports from the pulpit.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Book of Sports was a deliberate assault on the Puritan doctrine of the Lord's Day, and in 1633 an assault on the consciences of ministers, who were ordered to announce from the pulpit a permission they believed the fourth commandment forbade. When the crown commands a minister to preach against God's law, the answer is the apostles': “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29).

The corruption is not dead because the declaration was burned. The modern Christian Sunday, given over to sport and commerce after a morning service, is the Book of Sports without the king. The principle to recover is that the Lord's Day belongs to the Lord, the day John was “in the Spirit on the Lord's day” (Rev 1:10), and is to be kept as a delight in Him rather than in our own pleasure.

Usage

"“Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy” (Exo 20:8) — the commandment read after the declaration."

"“nor finding thine own pleasure” (Isa 58:13) — the answer to Sunday sports."

"“We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29) — the ministers who would not read it."
